title: Family Kinship, Dharma Companions
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: (Original excerpt from the Autobiographical Chronicle of Master Xuyun)

inline.s: (Original excerpt from the Autobiographical Chronicle of Master Xuyun)
Master Xuyun wrote in his chronicle:

blocks.text: The Second Year of Xuantong, Gengxu Year, at Age Seventy-One (1910)

inline.s: In the summer, a family letter came by way of Gushan
(Yongquan Monastery on Gushan in Fuzhou)
and was forwarded to Hunan
(Hunan Province)
— in the snap of a finger, fifty years had passed
(fifty years gone in an instant)

. I composed three poems, containing the lines: “This life holds only pure and spotless deeds; no other matter rests upon my heart.” “Long have I clean forgotten worldly things; let lingering habits not reach the clouds’ far edge.” Later Chen Rongchang, a secretary of the Hanlin Academy, composed the Record of the Verse Left by the Nun Miaojing, and it was carved in stone.
[Snap of a finger]
describes an extremely short span of time: the interval of a finger-snap
Appendix: The Record of the Verse Left by the Nun Miaojing
The bhikṣuṇī Miaojing, whose lay surname was Wang, was Master Yun’s stepmother
(his father’s concubine)
. Master Yun’s Dharma name was Guyan, his courtesy name Deqing, and his epithet Xuyun; he was a native of Xiangxiang, of the lay surname Xiao, and a descendant of Emperor Wu of Liang
(Emperor Wu of Liang)

. His father, Yutang, served on the staff of the prefect of Quanzhou in Fujian. His mother, Lady Yan, past forty and still childless, prayed to Guanyin, the Great Being, and conceived. His parents dreamed of a long-bearded man in a green robe, carrying Guanyin atop his head and riding a fierce tiger, who leapt onto the bed. The mother woke with a start, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room. Before long
(soon)
Master Yun was born; at birth he was a ball of flesh. His mother was sorely disappointed, and her breath choked and stopped. The next day
(the following day)
an old medicine-seller came, cut open the ball of flesh, and found a boy — this was Master Yun — and the stepmother raised him.
Master Yun by nature disliked eating
(eating)
meat; when somewhat older he was sent to school
(to study under a teacher)
. He had no taste for the Confucian books, but by nature loved the Buddhist scriptures. His father grew
(increasingly)
displeased and sternly reproved him. At seventeen, because
(on account of)
he was to carry on
(continuing the lines of both his father and his uncle)
the ancestral succession
tiāo
, to be heir)
, his father took two wives for him, one of the Tian family and one of the Tan family. Master Yun did not wish this, and fled to Gushan in Min
(Fujian Province)
, where he took the elder Miaolian as his teacher. In the jiazi year, the third year of Tongzhi
, when Xuyun was
his father died, and the stepmother thereupon led the two daughters-in-law into the Buddhist order as nuns. The Tian woman had long suffered from coughing
kǎ
blood, and four years after taking the tonsure
(four years after leaving home)
died of illness
mò
, to die)

. The Tan woman still lived; she was a nun on Guanyin Mountain in Xiangxiang, with the Dharma name Qingjie. She once wrote to Master Yun, saying that on the Laba day (the eighth of the twelfth month) of the jiyou year
, the eighth day of the twelfth month)
the stepmother passed away to the west. When she was on the verge of death
(at the point of death)
, she sat in full lotus
(the cross-legged posture)
, left a verse, and passed away. The verse reads:

What use is it to raise a son, I sigh? Once his wings are hard, he spreads them and takes flight; in pregnancy my life hung by a thread so nigh; once safely born, I thanked the gods with all my might.

Unwearying I nursed you through filth and pain; like a lion clasping its ball, I never let you go; but when the tender chick becomes a roc and flies, on whom can your aging, loving mother lean, for woe?

No brothers have you, and your father is gone; forsaking us, mother and wife, on whom shall we depend? This foolish love cannot release its longing for the child I raised; the more I brood, the sadder — how my tears descend.
[Brothers thin and cold]
You (Xuyun) have
neither an elder brother
nor
a younger brother
. [To rear (
jú
) and nurture] To raise and bring up.

Would I, a ghost-mother, set out to find my son? Lifting my eyes, only cloud-wreathed mountains wall on wall; if you can devote yourself to the great matter of birth and death, did not Pang Yun keep the Way, at home, after all?
[Pang Yun] A famous lay Chan practitioner of the Tang dynasty
known in the world as Layman Pang
[Did not Pang Yun keep the Way?] The meaning is: why do you not study Layman Pang, who practiced Chan while remaining at home, instead of abandoning your family and going against filial piety?

Worldly love and Dharma love — what difference in their worth? Even the mountain birds know to roost at the setting sun; though we once shared one vow to serve the Buddha’s house, daily I wash myself in the cold green mountain’s run.

You, my son, are early become a prince of the Empty One; the World-Honored One delivered even the aunt who raised him; grieving that this sahā world is naught but affliction, I now rest my heart and turn toward the Land of Bliss.
[My son is early become a prince of the Empty One
, and the World-Honored One once delivered his aunt
] My child
(Xuyun), you attained the Way long ago — why do you not come to deliver me? Remember that Śākyamuni Buddha likewise delivered the aunt who raised him!
[The World-Honored One once delivered his aunt]
Śākyamuni Buddha
opened the gate of skillful means for Mahāprajāpatī, the aunt who had raised him, permitting her to lead five hundred women of the Śākya clan into the monastic order,
and thereby
Buddhism gained its community of bhikṣuṇīs.
Another verse says:
Ever for love’s sake I clung to this dusty red; in greed and delusion I forgot my original face; eighty-odd years — all an illusory dream; ten thousand affairs turned empty, without a single trace.

Today I shed the burdens of this life, and gain the pure, wondrous body of the Lotus Land; you with the affinity, recite the Buddha’s name and go west; do not sink willingly in the bitter sea’s strand.

When Master Yun received the letter he was filled with both grief and joy — grief that he had not yet repaid the kindness of his upbringing, and joy that his stepmother, after more than forty years as a nun, had died with an unmuddled mind, leaving a verse and passing away, which was the sign of rebirth in the west.
In the eleventh year of the Republic
, in the summer of the renxu year, Chen Rongchang respectfully composed and inscribed this.
Appendix: The letter from the Nun Qingjie
(née Tan)

Since I last parted from your honored presence, my thoughts have ever turned to you with deep longing. But cloud-wreathed mountains block the way, and letters can scarcely pass; the fault of my negligence is due to
(this)
, and from afar I
(wish)
hope that you, the worthy one,
(Xuyun, styled Deqing)
the great monk, are at peace in all your comings and goings
(well and at ease)
, and that your Dharma body is healthy — how
(how very)

I pray for you from afar. I recall that you fled from your native home more than fifty years ago; waking or sleeping, not a moment passes without my longing for you. I do not know where your footsteps wander, or in what immortal land you dwell, and that I cannot attend upon you fills me with deep remorse
zè
, unease of heart)

This spring, in the first month, I heard from afar that you dwell in seclusion by the Min sea, at ease and content. Hearing this I could not but feel both grief and joy, yet I still do not know your actual whereabouts, and my anxious longing finds no rest. For I reflect that above, you have forsaken the kindness of your parents who raised you, and below, you have cast aside the bond with us, your wedded wives
(your original spouses)

; thinking on this in the still of night, how can your heart bear it? Moreover, now you have neither brothers, and our parents are aged; our own lot is unfortunate, and we have not been able to prosper the clan or continue the line — there is no one in the household to lean upon and no heir to carry on the ancestral line. Every time I recall this, I cannot keep my tears from streaming
cén
down in floods.
The Confucians take the Five Constants
(here referring to the father’s righteousness, the mother’s kindness, the elder brother’s friendliness, the younger brother’s respect, and the son’s filial piety)
as their Way. In olden times, the immortal of Xiang still delivered Lord Wen and his wife; and our Buddha, treating relatives and enemies alike, delivered Devadatta

(that is, Devadatta, son of King Dronodana and cousin of the Buddha. He left home and studied supernormal powers, possessed the thirty-two marks, and recited sixty thousand dharmas; for the sake of gain he committed the five grave sins, repeatedly tried to harm the Buddha, and fell into hell alive)
and Yaśodharā
(that is, Yaśodharā, the Buddha’s wife before he left home)
before all others. Are we, then, not karmically connected with you? Even if your thoughts no longer turn to your native place, you should still reflect on the toil
qú
of those who raised you. There is nothing we can do; I shall now briefly set forth the state of our family affairs.

[Five Constants] The five kinds of moral cultivation. First, they refer to benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and good faith. Second, they refer to the father’s righteousness, the mother’s kindness, the elder brother’s friendliness, the younger brother’s respect, and the son’s filial piety. [The immortal of Xiang still delivered Lord Wen and his wife] In olden times, Han Xiangzi (one of the legendary Eight Immortals, a grand-nephew of Han Yu) still delivered Han Yu (known in the world as “Lord Wen of Han”) and his wife to immortality.
[The toil (
qú
) of raising]
refers especially to the
pain and labor of parents rearing their children:
“Alas, alas, my parents, who bore and raised me with such toil.”
After you departed
(your honored person)
in haste, our kind father sent men to search for you in four directions but found no trace; his grief
tòng
, extreme sorrow)
remained in his heart, and he was constantly ill. He retired and returned home. After nursing his illness for more than a year, in the jiazi year
(the third year of Tongzhi,
, when Xuyun was
on the fourth day of the twelfth month, at the si hour
(nine to eleven in the morning)
he passed away. After the funeral was arranged, my aunt
(that is, the stepmother, née Wang)

led me and the young lady of the Tian family together into the Buddhist order. My aunt’s Dharma name was Miaojing; Tian Eying’s Dharma name was Zhenjie; and my name is Qingjie. The family affairs were all handed over to our uncle and aunt to manage, with much done in good works and public charity; I need not recount the rest. Eying coughed blood
(vomited blood)
, and after taking the black robes
(leaving home)
for four years
(four years)
she let go and returned to the west. In the yihai year
our uncle died of illness in Wenzhou. My eldest brother now governs
(holds office in)
Xining Prefecture, and Rongguo
(our cousin)
has gone to Japan with Eying’s third brother. Huaguo continues your line; as for Fuguo, since he left to follow you, no word of him has been seen.

The ancients said that great virtue leaves no heir. Though you are a monk reborn, yet you have suddenly cut off the incense of both ancestral shrines. Even if a bodhisattva delivers all beings, he cannot but let the ignorant slander him as lacking in filial duty. I myself have been lacking in filial duty; I have always admired your deep spiritual roots, your lofty aspiration and firm vows, like a lotus unstained by the mud. So why must you go far from your native village and suddenly forget your roots? The reason I write this letter in such pain is solely this.
Last winter
(last winter, the first year of Xuantong,
in the jiyou year, on the eighth day of the twelfth month, at the chen hour
(seven to nine in the morning)
, my aunt, née Wang
(the bhikṣuṇī Miaojing)
took her leave and returned to the west. In her final moments she sat in full lotus and spoke a verse
(see the Record of the Verse Left by the Nun Miaojing above)

; when the verse was done, she lowered her gaze and passed away in stillness. A wondrous fragrance lingered for days, and she sat upright and imposing, as if alive. Alas, though the world is but a dream, even a man of wood would weep! I send these few words so that you may know the state of our household affairs.
On the day this letter reaches you, please quickly pack and set out, with not a moment’s delay, and bring
(lead)
Fuguo home with you, so that Qingjie’s longing and eager hope
(devout hope)
and my utmost earnestness may not be in vain — that would be my deepest fortune. Moreover, now that the sacred teaching is withering
(now that the sacred teaching is in decline)
, the customs of Chu and Xia
(the traditional customs of China)

— how can you not know them? I bow and beg that my master, like the Venerable Kāśyapa, will shed his purple-gold light and be our companion in the Dharma. With a breast full of tears, for my whole life
(for the whole span of this life)
I shall keep this one hope. A thousand words cannot exhaust my humble thoughts; the meaning lies in what is left unsaid. Not a morning, not an evening
(every morning and every evening)
goes by without my boundless longing and prayer. Respectfully
(with respect)
I bow and inquire after your kind health, and beseech your clear discernment
(clear understanding)
; I will not go on
(I will not set everything down one by one)
You too, like the wild goose, left your native land; alone you soared into the sky and winged toward the south;
Pitiful the mate who shared your nest, still grieving on, while autumn wind across ten thousand li prolongs her woe.
I gaze until the moon at the sky’s edge fades, and a spring of tears floods my eyes;
I dwell upon the Xiang River’s shore, where the bamboo is already dappled with stains.
[The bamboo is already dappled with stains] Legend has it that when Shun died on his southern tour, his consorts Ehuang
and
Nüying embraced the bamboo between the rivers and wept bitterly; their tears stained the green bamboo, and when their tears were spent they died
From then on the bamboo bore spots
, hence it is called “Xiaoxiang bamboo” or “the bamboo of the Xiang consorts.”
You will surely attain the great Way, and your wisdom-karma will daily renew
Those once companions in the burning house are in truth the kinsfolk of the citadel of the Dharma.
[Burning house] The three realms are filled with turmoil and have no peace, like a burning house,
and so
the three realms are likened to a burning house.
The
Lotus Sutra
says
: “The three realms have no peace, being like a burning house.”
Written in tears and sobs, with a hundred prostrations, by your disciple Qingjie, a nun of Guanyin Mountain
At the gengxu
(the second year of Xuantong,
year, the nineteenth day of the second month.
